title: Centripetal Acceleration and Centripetal Force
notes: **Centripetal acceleration:** $a_c = v^2/r = r\omega^2$. It points toward the centre of the circle and changes the direction of velocity without changing its magnitude.
**Why 'centripetal' means centre-seeking:** without this inward acceleration, the object would move in a straight line by Newton's first law.
**Centripetal force:** $F_c = mv^2/r = mr\omega^2$. This is not a new type of force; it is the net inward force required for circular motion.
**Examples of centripetal force:** tension in a string for a conical pendulum, friction between tyres and road for a turning car, gravity for a satellite.
**Centrifugal force:** in a rotating frame, an outward pseudo force appears. It is not a real force but a consequence of inertia in a non-inertial frame.

**Derivation of $a_c$:** for a particle moving at speed $v$ in a circle, the velocity changes direction but not magnitude. For a small angle $d\theta$, the change in velocity $|d\vec{v}| = v\,d\theta$. Since $d\theta = ds/r = v\,dt/r$, the acceleration $a_c = |d\vec{v}|/dt = v^2/r$.
**No work done by centripetal force:** since $\vec{F}_c$ is perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, the power $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$. Centripetal force changes direction but never the kinetic energy.
**Banking and centripetal force:** on a banked road, the horizontal component of the normal reaction provides $F_c = N\sin\theta$. On an unbanked road, static friction provides it: $F_c = \mu_s N$.
**Satellite orbit:** for a satellite in circular orbit at radius $R$ from Earth's centre, $mv^2/R = GMm/R^2$, giving $v = \sqrt{GM/R}$. Larger orbits mean lower orbital speeds.
**Conical pendulum:** tension $T$ provides centripetal force $T\sin\theta = mv^2/r$, while its vertical component $T\cos\theta$ balances the weight.
**Unit analysis:** $[mv^2/r] = \text{kg} \cdot (\text{m/s})^2 / \text{m} = \text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2 = \text{N}$. The centripetal force formula is dimensionally consistent.
confusion: Centripetal force is not a new or special type of force. It is always one of the existing forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction, or their resultant) directed toward the centre.
Centrifugal force is a fictitious (pseudo) force that appears only in a rotating reference frame. In an inertial frame, it does not exist — the object merely tends to move in a straight line.
Centripetal force does no work because it is perpendicular to the velocity. An object in uniform circular motion has constant speed and constant kinetic energy.
The centripetal force $mv^2/r$ does not appear in free body diagrams as a separate force. The net of all real forces in the radial direction must equal $mv^2/r$.

As radius increases for a given speed, less centripetal force is needed ($F_c \propto 1/r$). But for a given angular velocity, more force is needed ($F_c \propto r$). Always check which variable is held constant.
practice: A 2 kg stone is swung in a vertical circle of radius 1.5 m at 6 m/s. Find the centripetal acceleration and centripetal force. Solution: $a_c = v^2/r = 36/1.5 = 24$ m/s$^2$. $F_c = ma_c = 2 \times 24 = 48$ N.

A car of mass 1200 kg turns a corner of radius 50 m at 20 m/s on a flat road. Find the friction force needed and the minimum coefficient of friction. Solution: $F_c = mv^2/r = 1200 \times 400/50 = 9600$ N. $f = \mu_s mg$, so $\mu_s = 9600/(1200 \times 9.8) = 0.816$.

A satellite orbits Earth at $R = 7000$ km from the centre. Earth's mass $M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ Nm$^2$/kg$^2$. Find the orbital speed. Solution: $v = \sqrt{GM/R} = \sqrt{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24} / 7 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{5.69 \times 10^7} = 7543$ m/s $\approx 7.5$ km/s.

A 0.5 kg mass is attached to a 1 m string and swings in a horizontal circle with the string at $60^{\circ}$ to the vertical. Find the tension, speed, and period. Solution: $T\cos 60^{\circ} = mg = 4.9$, so $T = 9.8$ N. $r = l\sin 60^{\circ} = 0.866$ m. $T\sin 60^{\circ} = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{Tr\sin 60^{\circ}/m} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 0.866 \times 0.866/0.5} = 3.83$ m/s. $T_{period} = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi \times 0.866/3.83 = 1.42$ s.

A washing machine drum of radius 0.25 m spins at 1200 RPM. Find the centripetal acceleration at the rim. Solution: $\omega = 1200 \times 2\pi/60 = 40\pi \approx 125.66$ rad/s. $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.25 \times 15791 = 3948$ m/s$^2 \approx 403g$. This enormous acceleration is how water is extracted from clothes.
universalFacts: Centripetal force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it never changes the kinetic energy or speed of the object — it only changes the direction of motion.
For any object in uniform circular motion, there must be a net inward force. If this force disappears, the object flies off tangentially in a straight line, not radially outward.

The fastest a planet can orbit at a given radius is the speed of light. For a black hole, the event horizon radius is where the required centripetal acceleration equals the speed of light divided by light-crossing time.

In the rotating reference frame of a carnival ride, passengers feel pushed outward (centrifugal force). In the inertial frame, they are simply being constrained to circular motion by the wall of the ride.
On Earth's surface, objects at the equator experience a centripetal acceleration of about $0.034$ m/s$^2$ due to Earth's rotation — about $0.3\%$ of $g$.
